newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Chirac bids to calm ruffled Belgian feathers.
newsitem.headline: Chirac bids to calm ruffled Belgian feathers.

text.p: Right-wing French President Jacques Chirac, forced to share his political bed with a left wing government, came to Belgium on Wednesday in a bid to smooth troubled diplomatic relations with his neighbour.

"We have, naturally, like all families, problems from time to time. When we reflect...it is practically nothing in relation to our economic, cultural and social riches, he said after meeting Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.
"There is between our countries a unity. When the important things come up we have the same point of view," Chirac added.
It was the first official visit by a French president to Belgium in nearly 14 years.
Chirac did not come to the meeting empty handed.

He told Dehaene that disputed documents relating to an alleged bribery scandal involving Belgian political parties and French industrialist Serge Dassault would be handed to Belgian investigators on Thursday.

Belgium has been increasingly impatient with the failure of the French authorities to cooperate in the investigation over the bribes allegedly paid to political parties in the late 1980s for contracts to refit Belgian F16 jet fighters.

Chirac also said that he would not be against a meeting -- perhaps at head of state level -- between France, Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany and the Netherlands to sort out a dispute over French unilateral insistence on maintaining border checks.
The French flouting of the so-called Schengen open border agreement has been a running diplomatic sore for some time.

Chirac was not apologetic for his country's action. He noted that in the past 18 months border controls had held 6,600 people and seized 254 kilograms of heroin and 15,000 capsules of the drug ecstasy.

"It is a dramatic affair. Drugs destroy families and people. Everything must be done to fight this scourge of our society," he said, noting that most of the seized drugs originated in the Netherlands and simply transited through northern Belgium.
Dehaene went along with the conciliatory tone, noting that Belgian anger was not with the aim but with the method.

There was even a semblance of reconciliation between the two over the shock closure of French carmaker Renault's plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels, although Dehaene repeated his view that the way the closure had been announced was not "modern".
However, he added that the matter was first and foremost a corporate affair and not one directly involving the French government despite the fact that it is the single largest shareholder.
The closure announcement at the end of February sparked a bitter diplomatic row between Belgium and France and a series of demonstrations in Brussels and Paris.

Despite the fact that the new left-wing French government led by Lionel Jospin had promised to review the closure decision, the definitive death of the profitable plant was confirmed late last month after an independent enquiry.

A handful of Vilvoorde workers tried to demonstrate at the airport where Chirac arrived in Belgium and later demonstrated noisily but peacefully near Brussels' Egmont Palace where Chirac and Dehaene met.
